That stage builds a full strategy-free LiveNodewith real data clients (build_bolt_v3_strategy_free_live_node_with_resolved_for_data_clients), connects them, runs, and stops — kernel Stopped, engine clients disconnected. Its kernel claims NT's once-per-process logger (log::set_boxed_logger; see NT crates/common/src/logging/logger.rs, the re-init comment). After the stage, the real node runs mute. Proof: evernstance>.log — including all three v0.1.7 session-one boots —04:45:06→04:45:21; 07-09: 03:33:32→03:33:38 "Event loop stopped"). Under v0.1.7 the stdout→journald sink survived (session one's 05:45 ERROR lines exist); under v0.1.9 both sinks die — zero journald lines across 19 minutes of live process after the launch-identity write at 03:33:38.

Both block_on on the main thread. NT's msgbus/cache/actorcrates/common/src/msgbus/mod.rs:94,197;crates/common/src/actor/registry.rs), and bolt's chainlink provider spawns its liveness supervisor onto NT's global runtime via get_runtime().spawn(...). Find that and both regressions likely share one root cause — and the fix is one change: stop running a   full LiveNode in-process before the real one (run the health stndalone ops reference-current-price-health subcommand already exists — or have the launcher own one process-lifetime initiali

Every production subscribe_* call in strategies/binary_oracle_edge_taker/subscriptions.rs is #[cfg(test)]-compiled-out, and record_reference_price_subscribe_event stores only under cfg(test) (production: let _ = event). The production subscription    path is structurally unexercisable by the current test suite — our review rounds caught none of this. Any fix must add

Investigation finished. Here is the verdict, then the execution brief for Codex.

## Verdict: two separate defects, one silencer — not one root cause

**Defect 1 — the mute node (the silencer).** Fully proven in NT source at the pinned rev. The launch chain's health probe builds a full trading node *inside the same process* as the real node. When the probe finishes and tears down, NT's logger shutdown (`logger.rs:1343-1380`) turns logging off **process-wide** (`log::set_max_level(Off)`) and kills the writer thread. The real node then tries to re-initialize logging, fails (the Rust `log` facade only accepts one logger per process, `logger.rs:931`), and NT's kernel silently "recovers" by attaching to the dead writer (`kernel.rs:278-296` — the comment even says this pattern is "common in tests"). Logging level is never restored, so every log line in the process becomes a no-op — that's why journald showed *nothing*, not even error spam. Important nuance the parallel session's owner-measured correction confirms: this is **not new in v0.1.9 — the node has been mute since v0.1.6**. v0.1.7 traded while equally mute.

**Defect 2 — the silent strategy plane (the real regression).** I finished the singleton sweep you asked for, and the probe is **not** the cause. At the pinned NT rev: every thread-local channel is re-bound by the second node *before* it builds its kernel, clock, and data clients (`builder.rs:421`, re-bound again at start, `node.rs:500/862`); the message bus is replaced per kernel; the actor registry is last-writer-wins; bolt's chainlink client captures its channel *after* the re-bind. And the decisive control: v0.1.7 ran the exact same probe-then-node sequence in one process and traded for an hour. So regression 2 lives in the bot code that changed between v0.1.7 and v0.1.9 — dominated by #1285's subscription rework, which had **never run live before this boot** (v0.1.8 died earlier in startup). Every warning it would have printed was eaten by defect 1.

**Proven by execution, not just reading:** all three subscription dispatch paths in the strategy are compiled out of test builds (`#[cfg(not(test))]`). I ran the new dispatch test at the Codex branch tip in an isolated worktree: it **fails with `commands=[]`** — the test suite is structurally blind to production subscriptions. That's why four review rounds missed this.

**One open question resolved:** the missing `signal_instrument_id`/`signal_venue` keys in the box config are **by design** — the archetype composes them from `[signal_data.primary]` and fails loudly if the client is unknown. Not a finding.

## State you should know about

A Codex session already started on branch `fix-live-boot-regressions` (4 commits, this morning 13:00–13:33 KST, tip `c9d613663`). Its core fix — running the health probe as a **subprocess** so it can never touch the real node's process — is exactly the right class fix. But the branch is incomplete: its own dispatch test is red (my run above), there's no strategy-side work, and one now-dead function is left in `main.rs`. The brief below continues that branch rather than restarting.

## Execution brief for Codex (relay when you're ready)

> **Branch:** continue `fix-live-boot-regressions` from `c9d613663`. Scope: kill the mute-node defect for good, make the production subscription path testable, and pin regression 2. Anchor all claims on symbols, not line numbers.
>
> **1. Keep the subprocess probe fix (`8fc9310ff`) and complete it.**
> - Add a failure-mode test: subprocess exits non-zero → the launch stage fails → `Start` never runs.
> - Add the logging-survival differential: a test that initializes NT logging, builds/stops/drops a strategy-free kernel in-process, then asserts a later kernel can still emit log lines. Prove it **red** against the old in-process pattern first (temp head with test but no fix — debug lane only, no manual full-CI dispatches), green with the subprocess fix.
> - Delete the now-dead `run_loaded_reference_current_price_health_with_resolved` in `main.rs` (its only production caller was the in-process stage).
> - Document in the PR body: the subprocess re-resolves secrets (a second SSM pass per launch) — accepted cost.
>
> **2. Un-gate production dispatch (class fix for the blindness).**
> Remove the `#[cfg(not(test))]` gates on the `subscribe_*`/`unsubscribe_*` calls in `strategies/binary_oracle_edge_taker/subscriptions.rs`. Tests must observe dispatch through the real NT seam by installing a recording `DataCommandSender` via `replace_data_cmd_sender` — the pattern already in `e45e2b050`. That turns the currently-red `strategy_on_start_dispatches_real_data_subscribe_commands` green for all three families (signal quotes, reference custom-data, RV sources). Where the test-only `record_*_subscribe_event` duplication becomes redundant, collapse to the one real seam.
>
> **3. Repo-blessed-profile derivation differential (may pin regression 2 before any boot).**
> A test that composes the real `prod-btc-5m` profile through the archetype (no synthetic fixtures) and asserts the derived subscription request lists are non-empty and name the expected sources: one chainlink reference source, the `[signal_data.primary]` pair, and the three enabled spot sources of `btc_usdt_midpoint_rv`. If this is red at the deployed rev, regression 2 is found offline. If green, the remaining fork (dispatched-but-died downstream) is decided by one logged boot after redeploy.
>
> **4. Fail loud on silently-empty startup.**
> `on_start` deriving zero subscriptions while the config declares sources must abort startup with an error, not warn-and-run. Same for the error→empty-`Vec` shape in `reference_price_subscription_requests`. (Loud halt, not a threshold — consistent with the standing no-gates rule.)
>
> Every new test follows differential discipline: prove it fails on the defective shape before proving it passes with the fix. One PR is fine if it stays reviewable; otherwise split 1 from 2–4.

Verified everything at the real PR head (`98449886a` — one merge-of-main newer than the head Codex quoted; no PR-side changes in the merge). The red/green proofs are genuine: the temp-head probe failed on exactly the right assertion ("the later kernel must leave the process logger enabled" — i.e., logger at `Off` after an in-process probe), and Debug Test passed at `4ccf4c0b7`. The core fix and the logging-survival differential are sound and prove the class invariant at the real seam.

On the three adversarial findings — I re-derived each against the head, and your instinct is mostly right. Two of the three should **not** be answered with more tests, and the right resolution **deletes more test code than it adds**:

**Finding 1 (HIGH, stubbed subprocess test) — confirmed, but the fix is a restructure, not a harness.** The test really does fabricate the error itself; the actual `output.status.success()` check has zero coverage — delete that line and everything stays green. The clean fix: move the status-check decision out of the spawn wrapper into a tiny pure function, and test *that* with a fabricated exit status (one ~5-line test). The spawn wrapper becomes too thin to get wrong. No subprocess test harness, no new machinery. The existing stubbed test stays as-is — it legitimately covers a different thing (stage error → Start never runs).

**Finding 2 (MEDIUM, weak source fence) — the observation is true, but its proposed fix violates your standing rule and I reject it.** Enumerating forbidden symbol names is the blacklist-that-never-terminates pattern; it would be decorative debt. The class closure belongs in **production behavior, at the boundary**: the real node should refuse to boot if process logging is dead (one check after kernel build — logging initialized and level not `Off` — abort loudly otherwise). That protects against *any* future in-process kernel, under any name, forever — and it's a behavior fix, not a test and not a gate. It also retroactively closes the exact hole that let the box run mute for three releases.

**Finding 3 (MEDIUM, JSON parsing) — confirmed, and the fix is deletion.** The parent-side report parsing duplicates the child's own contract: the child already validates the report and encodes pass/fail in its exit code. Worse, the child's stdout mixes NT log lines with the report, and the parser grabs the *first* `{` in that stream — a brace inside any boot log line makes a **healthy probe fail the launch**. It's net-negative reliability. Delete the parser, its two tests, and the two error variants (~100 lines gone); exit code is the contract, stdout forwards verbatim for the operator.

So the revision punch list for Codex is: delete the parser (−2 tests), extract the pure status-decision function (+1 tiny test), add the boot-time logging-alive check in the real node path and fold its assertion into the existing survival differential (no new test file). Net: fewer tests, fewer lines, one new production invariant. Optionally trim the always-true `parent_logger_alive` cell in the wiring test — it asserts nothing.

Two things to keep visible:

- **This PR does not bring trading back.** Per the owner-measured correction, v0.1.7 traded while equally mute — the logging fix is the diagnostic instrument. The strategy-plane regression (brief items 2–4: un-gate the `#[cfg(test)]`-compiled-out dispatch, the repo-blessed-profile derivation differential, fail-loud on zero derived subscriptions) is still open work.
- Current PR checks were still pending when Codex reported; I'm not claiming full CI green, and merge-readiness isn't mine to declare.

The three internal adversarial findings were independently re-verified against the pinned head. Adjudication:

`ops_launch_reference_health_subprocess_nonzero_aborts_before_start` fabricates `ChildExitedNonZero` inside its stage stub and never calls `run_reference_current_price_health_subprocess`. Deleting the `!output.status.success()` check leaves every test green.

Keep the existing chain test unchanged — it legitimately covers stage-error → `Start` never runs.

### F2 — observation CONFIRMED, proposed fix REJECTED; boundary fix required instead
The finding that the source fence would miss a future in-process kernel under a new name is true. The proposed fix (enumerate forbidden `build_*live_node`/kernel symbols in the pre-`Start` path) is declined: forbidden-name enumeration never terminates and is standing-rule-banned in this repo. The fence stays as the cheap tripwire it is.

**Required class closure (production behavior, not a test):** the real node must refuse to boot when process logging is dead. After the real node's kernel is built and before it runs, verify NT logging is initialized and `log::max_level() != LevelFilter::Off`; abort the boot with an explicit error otherwise. Assert the new abort inside the existing survival differential's red shape; no new test file.

`parse_reference_current_price_health_subprocess_report` scans the child's stdout for the first `{` and parses one JSON value from there. The child's stdout is NT log lines + the final report; a brace inside any boot log line fails a healthy launch (`ReportUnparseable`). The parse also duplicates the child's own contract — the child already validates the report and encodes pass/fail in its exit code (`print_reference_current_price_health_report` errors on unobserved sources → non-zero exit).

**Required fix:** delete the parser, its two unit tests, and the `ReportMissing`/`ReportUnparseable` variants. Child exit code is the single contract; keep forwarding stdout/stderr verbatim.

`parent_logger_alive` in `ops_launch_reference_health_stage_then_start_keeps_parent_logging_boundary_alive` is set `true` and never mutated — the assert is decorative. Drop the cell or the assert.

- Parent buffers child output (`Command::output()`), so the probe's logs surface only after the child exits (~15–20s) and there is no parent-side timeout. Parity with the in-process stage (the child owns the same run/observation timeouts); note only.

## Owner review — round 2: all round-1 findings FIXED, no new blockers

**Pinned head:** `4101ec4fa41a280b3588250ac46e158596f572ca`. Full-PR re-review (round 1 = comment 4922776413). Revision delta vs round-1 head: 101 insertions / 120 deletions — net smaller, as required.

Unit test drives the real function with `ExitStatusExt::from_raw(0)` → `Ok` and `from_raw(256)` (exit code 1) → `Err` naming the subprocess. Signal terminations also map to `Err` via `status.success()`. The previously-uncovered abort branch is now covered without any subprocess harness.

**F2 — FIXED.** New production invariant `assert_bolt_v3_logging_ready_for_run()` (`log::max_level() != Off` and error records enabled) wired into `run_built_node` before the runtime is built — i.e., after the real node's kernel init, before it runs. Proven both ways: the survival differential's new `poisoned-parent` child mode **constructs** the real poisoned state (builds, stops, drops a strategy-free kernel in-process) and asserts the guard aborts naming `max_level=Off`; the entrypoint fence pins the guard's position inside `run_built_node` ahead of runtime construction. **What I verified at the exact head `4101ec4fa`:**

- **All three findings are genuinely fixed**, and I checked the substance, not just the claims. The parser and its error variants, tests, and audit entries are fully deleted. The exit-status check now lives in a small standalone function with a test that drives it with real exit statuses (including the "exit code 1" encoding, and crash-by-signal also maps to failure). The new boot guard sits in exactly the right place — after the node's kernel is built (where poisoning would show) and before it runs — and the proof test doesn't simulate the failure, it *builds and drops a real kernel* to poison the process and confirms the guard aborts naming the dead logger.
- **The revision shrank the PR**: 101 lines added, 120 removed. Your test-debt concern was honored.
- **CI evidence is real**: the four gate runs plus the second automatic cycle are all green at the exact head — I read each conclusion myself. One honesty note in the review: the "Debug Test" run Codex cited reports main's commit, not the PR head, so it's auxiliary; the exact-head gate runs are the evidence.
- One intended side effect, documented in the review: a node configured to bypass logging entirely will now also refuse to boot. For a live-money bot that's the correct behavior — running blind is the thing we just banned.

**Now it's your move, two things:**

1. **#1310**: if you're satisfied, approve with the sp-reviewer account and comment `@mergifyio queue`. (I don't declare merge-ready — state and evidence above, decision yours. External model rounds are also your call; my take is this PR is small and mechanically proven enough that they'd add little.)
2. **The second brief** (strategy plane — the actual trading blocker): relay it to a Codex session if you haven't. It doesn't depend on #1310, but both must be merged before we redeploy and do the one logged boot that finally pins regression 2.

The box stays stopped until both land.
what's the second brief for? I thought you needed the logger to identify the root cause

Fair question — the second brief isn't "fix the root cause we haven't found yet." None of its three tasks require knowing the cause. Here's what each is for:

1. **Restore the test suite's eyesight (Task 1).** Right now, no test in the repo can see whether the strategy actually subscribes to anything — the production subscription calls are compiled out of test builds. I proved this by running Codex's own test: it records zero commands. This has to be fixed *no matter what* the root cause turns out to be — because once we do find the bug, the fix needs a regression test, and today such a test is impossible to write.

2. **Try to find the root cause for free, offline (Task 2).** One suspect is that the strategy derives an *empty* subscription list from our real production config — a code/config mismatch, which would reproduce on a laptop with no box involved. This task runs the real prod config through startup in a test. If it fails: root cause found, no boot needed for diagnosis. If it passes: we've eliminated half the possibilities, and the logged boot settles the rest.

3. **Ban this failure mode from ever being silent again (Task 3).** Same idea as the "refuse to boot mute" guard in PR #1310: a strategy that starts up subscribed to *nothing*, while its config says it should be subscribed to things, should refuse to run — loudly. That's worth having even after the current bug is dead.

So the logger is still the final discriminator — you're right about that. The second brief just makes that one supervised boot *count*: either the offline test finds the bug first and the boot becomes pure verification, or the boot happens with a node that can now both log *and* fail loudly, so whatever it shows is unambiguous.

There is a legitimate alternative ordering, to be fair: merge #1310 alone, start the box, and do a purely diagnostic boot now — it's safe, since this failure mode places zero orders. That gets live evidence a few hours sooner. I still recommend brief-first, because Codex cycles are cheap and your supervised boots aren't — one boot that diagnoses-or-verifies beats two. But if you want the answer today, say so and we'll boot first.
so should we do task 2, 3 together?

Yes — 2 and 3 belong together. They're two halves of the same property: Task 2 writes the test that says "our real config must produce a non-empty subscription list at startup," and Task 3 makes the running node enforce that same property loudly. Same code region, same review cycle — splitting them would be pure overhead. There's even a natural sequence inside the work: Codex writes the Task 2 test first, and if it comes up red against the deployed code, we've found the bug and the rest of the PR becomes its fix.

The real question is whether Task 1 (un-gating the dispatch calls so tests can see real subscriptions) rides along or follows. My recommendation: keep it in the same PR. Reasons: it's the same file and seam, and it upgrades the Task 2/3 tests from "checks the list is computed" to "checks the subscriptions are actually sent" — which is the level this incident happened at. The list-computation could be perfect and the dispatch still broken; only Task 1 lets a test tell the difference.

If you want the smallest possible first step, the acceptable split is: 2+3 now, 1 immediately after. What's not acceptable is dropping 1 — the whole reason four review rounds missed this bug is that the dispatch path is invisible to tests, and that stays true until Task 1 lands.

So: relay the brief as-is (one PR, all three tasks, Task 2's test written first). If Codex reports the Task 2 test is red at the deployed rev, we'll know the root cause before the box ever starts.
generate the brief 2+3

Here's the brief for the 2+3 PR, copy-paste ready:

> **Brief: prove startup subscription derivation against the real production config, and make empty-derivation fail loud — #1179 campaign, regression 2, part 1 of 2.**
>
> **Context.** On the 07-09 v0.1.9 live boot the strategy started "successfully" but subscribed to nothing — zero quotes, zero orders — and every warning was swallowed by the now-fixed logger defect (PR #1310). The subscription *dispatch* seam is being made test-visible in a separate follow-up PR; **do not remove any `#[cfg(not(test))]`/`#[cfg(test)]` gates in this PR.** This PR works at the derivation level, which is fully visible to tests today.
>
> **Task A — derivation differential against the repo-blessed config (write this first).**
> Add a test that loads the real composed `prod-btc-5m` configuration through the archetype (`bolt_v3_archetypes/binary_oracle_edge_taker.rs` — the real path that composes `signal_venue`/`signal_instrument_id` from `[signal_data.primary]`; no synthetic fixtures) and checks the three startup derivation surfaces on the constructed strategy:
> - `reference_price_subscription_requests()` — non-empty, and its sources match exactly the enabled sources declared under `[reference_current_price]` in the loaded config;
> - `signal_instrument_id()` / `signal_client_id()` — both `Some`, matching the config's `[signal_data.primary]` pair;
> - `context.realized_volatility_{quote,trade,index}_subscription_requests_for_surface(realized_volatility_surface_id)` — union non-empty, covering the enabled sources of the configured surface.
>
> Derive every expected value from the loaded config in the test — never retype instrument/venue literals. **Run this test first at the deployed rev `b1e7ed34c`.** If it is red there: STOP, report the failure verbatim — that is the live regression's root cause and the PR pivots to fixing it. If green: state that explicitly in the PR body ("derivation is not the defect at the deployed rev") and continue to Task B.
>
> **Task B — fail loud on silently-empty startup.**
> Today a strategy can complete `on_start` having derived zero subscriptions, with only invisible warnings. Change the behavior:
> - `on_start` must return an error (failing node startup) when the config declares subscription sources but the derived request set is empty — reference, signal, and RV families each count.
> - `reference_price_subscription_requests()`'s error branch (`build_reference_price_subscription_requests` fails → currently `log::error!` + empty `Vec`) must propagate the error instead of degrading to empty.
> - The RV "no enabled subscribable sources" warn-only block in `subscribe_realized_volatility_sources` becomes part of the same startup error when the surface is configured.
>
> Loud abort only — no thresholds, no new config knobs, no fallback behavior. Differential discipline: write each Task B test first and prove it red against the current warn-and-continue behavior (temp head with test but no fix, debug lane), then green with the fix.
>
> **Rules.** One PR. Do not touch the dispatch `cfg` gates, the retry machinery in `on_time_event`, or unrelated subscription code. Zero manual full-CI dispatches — debug lane iterates, the merge queue is the gate. PR body: pinned head SHA, red/green run links, and the explicit Task A verdict at `b1e7ed34c`. No close-keywords referencing #1179. Report back with the pinned head and evidence; full-scope owner review follows.

Two notes for you: Task A doubles as the free root-cause probe — if it's red at the deployed rev, we've found the bug on a laptop, no boot needed. And the Task 1 follow-up (un-gating dispatch so tests see real subscriptions) stays queued right behind this; I'll hold it in the ledger so it doesn't get lost.

content.text:
Review done and posted: https://github.com/seungpyoson/bolt-v2/pull/1316#issuecomment-4924896467 — **no blockers**. And with #1310 now merged, the silencer fix plus the "refuse to boot mute" guard are on main.

The headline from #1316 isn't the code — it's the diagnostic result. I verified the deployed-rev proof at the commit level: the temp head sits directly on the deployed code, its only change besides the test is making one function visible to tests, and the test **passed**. That means: given our real production config, the deployed code computes the correct, non-empty list of things to subscribe to. **The bug is not in the config or the derivation.** Regression 2 lives further downstream — either the subscriptions never get *sent* (the dispatch seam that's still invisible to tests), or they're sent and something between the engine and the venues drops them.

I also verified the fail-loud half properly: the red run failed on exactly the four new tests before the fix existed, green at the exact head, and the guard runs before any timers are registered — so a strategy that would start blind now refuses to start instead.

What's left, in order:

1. **You, on #1316**: mark it ready for review, approve with sp-reviewer, `@mergifyio queue`. My round is clean; as always, merge-ready is your call.
2. **After #1316 merges**: relay the Task-1 brief (un-gating the dispatch calls so tests can see real subscriptions). It edits the same file as #1316, so it goes second, not in parallel — say the word when #1316 is in and I'll hand you the blurb.
3. **Then**: v0.1.10 build, redeploy, and the one supervised boot. Given what we now know, that boot is the decisive measurement: logging alive, startup either aborts loudly or subscribes — and if quotes still don't flow, the logs will show whether commands died at the engine or at the venues.
should we get reviews from external reviewers?

My recommendation: not for #1316 — save the external round for the regression-2 fix PR that comes after the boot.

The reasoning. The full relay pipeline (GPT/GLM/Kimi packets, you ferrying them by hand) earned its keep on the big campaign PRs — reconciler, settlement, exit valuation — where the behavior surface was wide, money was involved, and it caught things I missed. #1316 doesn't fit that profile: it's two-thirds test code, the production change is ~100 contained lines, and the two claims that matter are already proven mechanically rather than by judgment — the deployed-rev proof passed on code that differs from production by one visibility keyword, and the fail-loud tests were red before the fix and green after. An external panel re-reads what the runs already proved. (#1310 is merged, so the question is moot there — and it got an internal adversarial pass plus my adjudication anyway.)

The one question on #1316 where an outside eye has any real value: **could the new startup abort fire on a legitimately-configured deployment** — i.e., did we just build a false-positive boot blocker? I've checked the shapes (it only aborts when the config *declares* sources but derives nothing, and the real prod profile passes), but this is the kind of "adversarial reading of semantics" externals are good at. If you want cover on exactly that, two cheap options instead of the full round:

- Ask the Codex session for an internal adversarial review of #1316 scoped to that one question, like it did for #1310 — costs you nothing but a prompt, and I'll adjudicate whatever it finds.
- Or a single GLM pass (the one metered API we allow) with that one question, rather than the four-model relay.

Where I *would* bring the full external pipeline back: the PR that fixes regression 2 once the boot names it (that's live trading behavior), the Task-1 un-gating PR if it ends up changing any dispatch semantics rather than just visibility, and anything touching order/money paths before session two. That keeps the heavy process where the risk actually is.

• Findings

  No blocking findings found in the internal adversarial review.

  Reviewed the PR #1316 diff against origin/main, covering 4 files:

  - src/strategies/binary_oracle_edge_taker/mod.rs
  - src/strategies/binary_oracle_edge_taker/subscriptions.rs
  - src/strategies/binary_oracle_edge_taker/tests/reference_price.rs
  - docs/bolt-v3/research/runtime-literals/bolt-v3-runtime-literal-audit.toml

  The startup guard matches the brief: reference derivation errors now propagate, declared-but-empty reference/signal/RV derivations fail on_start, and
  dispatch #[cfg] gates plus on_time_event dispatch remain untouched.

  Residual risk: PR-triggered checks were still pending at review time (source-fence-static, bvs-clippy, bvs-test archive, ci-policy), though no failures were
  present. The sidecar reviewer did not return before timeout and was closed, so this review is based on direct inspection.
That matches my round-1 verdict — two independent passes, no blockers. Let me check whether those pending checks have finished so you can act on current state.

content.text:
Merge confirmed (`c66b68430`). Both halves of the campaign's part 1 are now on main: the node can't run mute, and it can't start silently subscribed to nothing.

Here's the Task-1 blurb, copy-paste ready:

> **Brief: make production subscription dispatch visible to tests — #1179 campaign, regression 2, part 2 of 2.** Start from current `main` (must include #1316's merge `c66b68430`).
>
> **Context.** #1316 proved the strategy *derives* the correct subscription requests from the real production config. What remains untestable is whether those requests are actually *dispatched* into NT: every production `subscribe_*`/`unsubscribe_*` call in `src/strategies/binary_oracle_edge_taker/subscriptions.rs` is `#[cfg(not(test))]`-gated, so test builds compile the dispatch out. Proven red previously: a recording-sender test on the old branch `fix-live-boot-regressions` (commit `e45e2b050`) fails with `commands=[]`. This PR removes that blindness. It is visibility work — do not change any dispatch semantics, ordering, or the fail-loud guards #1316 added.
>
> **Task 1 — un-gate the dispatch calls.** Remove the `#[cfg(not(test))]` / `#[cfg(test)] let _ = …` pairs on the dispatch calls in `subscriptions.rs` — all families: reference-price custom data, signal quotes, RV quotes/trades/index, and the resolution boundary subscribe/unsubscribe paths. Production code paths must be identical before and after; only test builds change.
>
> **Task 2 — one seam for test observation, installed once.** Critical hazard: once un-gated, every test that drives `on_start`/`on_stop` will reach NT's `get_data_cmd_sender()`, which panics when no sender is installed. Install the sender in the shared test fixture (the `register_test_strategy` helper), not per-test: a recording `DataCommandSender` via `nautilus_common::runner::replace_data_cmd_sender` (the `e45e2b050` pattern — cherry-pick or reimplement). Sweep the existing strategy test suite for panics from this change and fix them only via the fixture — no per-test sender plumbing.
>
> **Task 3 — the dispatch differential.** Land the test `strategy_on_start_dispatches_real_data_subscribe_commands` (salvage from `e45e2b050` or rewrite): `on_start` must enqueue real `DataCommand::Subscribe`s for all three startup families, asserted against the recording sender. Prove it red at a temp head containing the test but not the un-gating (expect `commands=[]`), then green at the PR head. Where the test-only `record_*_subscribe_event` bookkeeping becomes fully redundant with the real seam, collapse it — one seam, one recorder; if any recorder still carries assertions the seam can't express, keep it and say so in the PR body.
>
> **Rules.** One PR. No changes to dispatch semantics, the `on_time_event` retry machinery, or #1316's guards. Zero manual full-CI dispatches; debug lane iterates; the merge queue is the gate. PR body: pinned head SHA plus red/green run links. No close-keywords referencing #1179. After merge, the old branch `fix-live-boot-regressions` is fully superseded (its subprocess fix shipped as #1310, its test salvaged here) — note that in the PR body so the owner can delete the branch.

After this merges: v0.1.10 build, redeploy, one supervised boot. Logging alive, startup loud, dispatch observable — whatever that boot shows, it's the answer on regression 2.
so what is this? why are we doing this?

Fair question — here's the plain version.

**What happened live:** the bot started up, looked healthy, but never asked for any market data. No prices in, so no trades out. And nothing caught it — not the test suite, not four rounds of code review.

**Why nothing caught it:** the few lines of code where the bot actually *asks* for data are marked with a compile switch that removes them whenever the code is built for testing. So every test that "checks startup" has been checking a version of the bot with the asking-step deleted. Tests always pass, because the step that can fail isn't there during the test. It's like a fire drill where the alarm is unplugged for the drill — drills always succeed, and the one real fire goes undetected.

**What we've established so far:** the config is right, and the bot computes the correct "shopping list" of data to ask for (that was #1316 — proven against the real production config). So the failure is somewhere between "list computed" and "data arrives" — which is precisely the stretch of code the tests can't see.

**What this PR does:** removes that compile switch so tests run the real asking-step, and adds the one test that says "when the bot starts, it must actually send these requests." We proved that test fails today with "zero requests sent" — that's the blindness, demonstrated.

**Why bother before the boot:** two reasons. First, whatever the root cause turns out to be, the fix will need a test proving it stays fixed — and today that test is impossible to write. Second, it shrinks what the boot has to tell us: with this in place, if the boot still shows no data, we'll know our code did its part and the problem is at the venue/connection layer — instead of still wondering whether the bot ever asked.

It's the last piece of scaffolding. After it merges: build v0.1.10, redeploy, one supervised boot — and that boot gives us the answer.

Review posted — **request changes**: https://github.com/seungpyoson/bolt-v2/pull/1321#issuecomment-4926933130

The core of the PR is right, and I verified the deep parts hold up: the un-gating changes nothing in production (statements verbatim, same order), and the test fixture watches subscriptions at the *exact same connection point* production uses — I traced both sides into NT's source to confirm they're mirror images. The red proof is genuine too.

But two blockers:

1. **The PR body says `Closes #1179`.** Merging it would auto-close the whole campaign issue, which must stay open through session two. One-line deletion.

2. **The PR breaks 10+ existing tests — and nobody had run them.** Because the PR is a draft (drafts skip the heavy test lane here) and Codex stopped at the two-probe cap, there was no green run anywhere. So I ran the full strategy test module myself at the PR head: 10 adverse-path harness tests crash instantly, and the run aborted before reaching 380 more. The cause is instructive: those tests set up a "ready to trade" strategy in an order that asks for subscriptions *before* the strategy is registered with the trading engine. The old compile switches silently deleted that ask during tests — so the wrong ordering never mattered. Un-gate it, and NT rightfully panics. It's a latent bug in the test fixtures that this PR's honesty exposed. The fix is one change in the shared fixture (register first, then set up), not ten per-test patches — and the revision must prove the *entire* module green, not just the new tests.

Worth saying plainly: this failure is the PR doing its job. The whole point was "tests should see what production really does" — and the very first full run under that rule caught real ordering bugs that have been invisible since the harness was written.

Relay the review to the Codex session; I'll re-review the full PR at the new head when it lands.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""v0.1.10 install on bolt box: download, sha-verify, backup, install, regen+verify config.

Runs as root via SSM. Arg1 = expected sha256 of the new binary.
"""
import hashlib
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import time

S3_BIN = "s3://bolt-deploy-artifacts/artifacts/bolt-v2/v0.1.10/bolt-v2"
TMP = "/tmp/bolt-v2-v0110"
DEST = "/opt/bolt-v2/bolt-v2"
CFG_ROOT = "/opt/bolt-v2/config"


def run(cmd):
    print("+", " ".join(cmd), flush=True)
    subprocess.run(cmd, check=True)


def sha256(path):
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(1 << 20), b""):
            h.update(chunk)
    return h.hexdigest()


def main():
    expected = sys.argv[1]
    state = subprocess.run(
        ["systemctl", "is-active", "bolt-v2"], capture_output=True, text=True
    ).stdout.strip()
    print("service state before install:", state, flush=True)
    if state == "active":
        sys.exit("bolt-v2.service is ACTIVE - refusing to install over a running node")

    run(["aws", "s3", "cp", S3_BIN, TMP])
    got = sha256(TMP)
    if got != expected:
        sys.exit(f"sha mismatch: got {got} expected {expected}")
    print("download sha256 verified:", got, flush=True)

    ts = time.strftime("%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ", time.gmtime())
    bak = f"{DEST}.bak-pre-v0110-{ts}"
    shutil.copy2(DEST, bak)
    print("backup:", bak, "sha256:", sha256(bak), flush=True)

    shutil.copy2(TMP, DEST)
    run(["chmod", "755", DEST])
    print("installed sha256:", sha256(DEST), flush=True)

    run([DEST, "ops", "generate-live-config", "--profile", "prod-btc-5m", "--config-root", CFG_ROOT])
    run([DEST, "ops", "verify-live-config", "--profile", "prod-btc-5m", "--config-root", CFG_ROOT])
    print("INSTALL OK", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

content.text:
Box stopped, everything recorded. Here's where we stand:

## Regression 2 is solved — one boot, exactly as designed

**The cause was never in our code. Binance changed their wire protocol.** Their servers bumped the binary-encoding schema from version 4 to 5 sometime between July 7 (when v0.1.7 traded fine) and July 9 (the silent boot). Our pinned NT Binance adapter has version 4 hard-baked into generated code. The connection handshake fails, and because one required data client can't connect, NT **never starts the trading brain at all** — while still labeling the node "Running." Nothing ever subscribed because nothing ever asked.

Every mystery from the incident collapses into this one line: the four "independently dead" feeds (one upstream cause — the trader never started), the still-flowing instrument refreshes (Polymarket's client connected fine on its own), the "Running" state (NT's mislabel), and the total silence (the error *was* logged — into the logger the old probe had killed). It also overturns one earlier conclusion: we'd inferred "the strategy started, so the bug is in subscriptions." False — NT reports Running even when the trader never started. That inference cost us; now it's on record.

**And the campaign machinery paid for itself in one boot:** launch chain green, probe isolated in its own process with its logs visible, the real node's logger alive for the first time since v0.1.6 — and the root cause sitting in the journal in plain text, 16 seconds after startup. Compare: three days of blind forensics last time.

## Deploy record

v0.1.10 tagged and installed (checksums verified end-to-end, v0.1.9 backed up on-box), config regenerated and validated — all safety invariants intact. Service and box are **stopped**; evidence preserved in the journal.

## Next

Two-part fix, one brief, which I'll prepare next:
1. **The Binance schema fix** — rule one is check the vendor's docs and NT upstream *first*: Binance may honor requested-v4 during a deprecation window, and NT upstream has likely already regenerated v5 bindings we can port rather than hand-roll.
2. **Close the fail-open** — a node whose trader never started must abort the launch loudly, same family as the boot-aborts-if-mute guard. That's the structural change that turns any future vendor surprise into a 30-second diagnosis.

This fix touches live trading's data plane, so per our standing line it gets the full external review round. Want me to start the vendor-docs/NT-upstream investigation now?
yes - give me the prompt for that

Here's the prompt, copy-paste ready for a Codex session:

> **Brief: Binance SBE schema v4→v5 outage — investigate first, then fix — #1179 campaign, regression-2 root cause.**
>
> **Context.** The 2026-07-10 04:50Z diagnostic boot of v0.1.10 (box journal, evidence preserved) pinned the live incident's root cause:
> ```
> [ERROR] Failed to connect data client: failed to request Binance exchange info:
>         SBE decode error: Schema version mismatch: expected 4, was 5
> DataEngine.check_connected() == false
> [ERROR] Not starting trader: engine client(s) not connected
> ```
> Binance bumped their spot REST SBE schema version server-side between 07-07 and 07-09. Our pinned NT (`6be5a5094716790a8ca2875445fde4fa2586107e`) hard-pins schema 3:4 in generated code — `crates/adapters/binance/src/spot/sbe/generated/mod.rs`, sent as `X-MBX-SBE: 3:4` per `spot/http/client.rs`. One failed data client ⇒ NT never starts the trader ⇒ the entire strategy plane sat silent on 07-09. Separately: NT sets `NodeState::Running` even when the trader was never started (engine-connect timeout path in `crates/live/src/node.rs`) — a fail-open we must close on the bolt side.
>
> **Phase 1 — investigation only. NO code. Deliver a written verdict, then STOP for owner review.**
> 1. **Vendor docs first.** Read Binance's official spot API docs/changelog on SBE: does the server honor a requested older schema (`X-MBX-SBE: 3:4`) during a deprecation window, or is v4 already sunset? What exactly is in schema 3:5 vs 3:4? Cite exact URLs and quote the deprecation-policy text verbatim. Do not probe the API before reading the docs; after reading, one live check of the public `exchangeInfo` endpoint (no keys needed) to confirm observed server behavior for both requested versions is allowed — capture the raw responses as fixtures.
> 2. **NT upstream.** Search `nautechsystems/nautilus_trader` commits/PRs after our pin for regenerated Binance spot SBE v5 bindings or version-negotiation handling. Identify the minimal upstream change-set and assess: does it cherry-pick cleanly onto our pin? What else does it drag in?
> 3. **Options table** with trade-offs, recommendation-first:
>    (a) port the proven upstream fix onto our pin (preferred per the port-over-greenfield rule, if clean);
>    (b) full NT pin bump — enumerate everything else it pulls in and the re-validation surface;
>    (c) request-v4-during-deprecation-window if the docs confirm it's honored (buys time, not a fix — pair with (a) or (b));
>    (d) local hand-rolled adapter patch — last resort only, justify or reject.
>    Config-level workarounds (swapping the Binance signal source to another venue) are out of scope — that changes measured strategy inputs.
> 4. **Red-proof design.** Propose the differential: a decode test against a captured real v5 `exchangeInfo` payload that fails on current code and passes with the fix.
>
> **Phase 2 — after the owner relays the go on a chosen option.** Two PRs expected:
>    - **PR-A (SBE fix):** the chosen option, with the captured-fixture red/green differential. All vendor knowledge stays in the adapter/dependency layer — nothing Binance-specific leaks into bolt code.
>    - **PR-B (launch invariant):** bolt's launch must treat "trader not started" as a **launch failure** — if NT completes startup without the trader running (the engines-not-connected path), the process exits non-zero with a named error instead of idling as a trader-less "Running" node. Same invariant family as the existing boot-aborts-if-mute guard; prove red against the current fail-open shape (the 07-10 journal is the live repro), green with the abort. No thresholds, no retries-with-fallback — loud abort only.
>
> **Rules.** Phase 1 output is a report, not code. The documentation uses a hypothetical timeline but doesn't explicitly state the current production schema ID and version.

When clients request a deprecated schema via the `X-MBX-SBE` header:

content.text:
All claims verified independently — and everything converges. My recommendation: **approve (a), and yes to PR-B as specified.**

Here's what I confirmed with my own hands, not from the report:

1. **Binance's official policy** (their SBE FAQ, quoted): a deprecated schema is supported "for at least 6 months after deprecation," but during that window responses are "encoded in the highest compatible schema" — meaning even when you ask for v4, **they send v5** and expect your decoder to tolerate it. So the real defect in our pinned NT is that its decoder demanded an exact version match, violating the vendor's own compatibility contract. This wasn't Binance breaking us; it was our adapter being stricter than the protocol allows.

2. **The upstream fix is exactly the right shape** — I read the actual staged changes: it keeps requesting `3:4` (deliberately, so it works on servers mid-rollout), regenerates the codecs to v5, and — the important part — relaxes the decoder to accept *any* version within schema 3. That makes us tolerant of this bump *and the next one*. It's the class fix, not a patch.

3. **The port is empirically clean**: I ran the cherry-pick onto our exact pin myself — all 8 code files applied without conflict; the only collision is upstream's changelog file, which a port drops anyway.

4. **Why not (b)**: bumping the whole NT pin to current upstream drags in ~3 weeks of unrelated churn — an order-event serialization rework, WebSocket trading-signature changes, futures fixes — a big re-validation surface at exactly the moment we want minimal motion before session two. Do (b) later as its own deliberate upgrade, not under incident pressure.

Mechanics for (a): a fork branch (our pin + the one cherry-picked commit, changelog dropped), and `Cargo.toml` repointed to that fork revision — every other line of NT stays byte-identical to what's been running.

So: relay "approved: (a), PR-B proceeds as specified" to the Codex session. The red proof should be the captured real v5 payload failing against the current decoder; both PRs get the full external review round, and after they land: rebuild, redeploy, and this time the boot should end with quotes — and session two starts.

   README (spot/sbe/README.md, "Version compatibility") concedes exactly this.

   Concrete scenario: Binance ships schema 3:6 that appends one field to the depth or trades message fixed block (the part before the repeating group). The
   runtime block_length grows, but header.validate() no longer rejects it, so the body decoder reads the appended fixed-field bytes as the group header
   (block_len, count). Outcome is a garbage count → either a silently corrupt order book/trade list fed downstream, or read_group walking off the buffer.
   Pre-port this was a hard VersionMismatch { expected: 5, actual: 6 }; post-port it enters the body. decode_klines shares the same fixed-offset pattern and
   is worth the same scrutiny.

   instrument-load path that actually fired). So this is not on Bolt's hot path today — flagging because the "schema id 3 ⇒ safe" invariant is now
   load-bearing for the whole adapter, and any future REST depth/trades consumer (or reuse of this pin) would silently misread a bumped fixed block. Recommend
   either a fixed-offset→runtime-block_length advance in depth/trades/klines, or a documented "REST depth/trades not used by this deployment" assertion so the
   latent defect can't quietly become live.

   A2 — Dual fixture copies are identical now but unguarded against future drift. (Informational.)

Critically, the strict version check that was removed was the defect — the pre-existing README's "Forward compatibility note" already documented that the parsers use block_length to skip unknown trailing fields; the version gate was a redundant hard-fail that broke on a valid additive bump. B2. Abort path resource stranding / evidence-store skip — NONE.
capture_guards.shutdown().await (prb_live_node.rs:2650) and drain_decision_evidence_shutdown (prb_live_node.rs:2718-2720) run unconditionally after the watchdog returns, before the outcome match and after it respectively — for every outcome variant including TraderNotStarted and the TraderNotStartedInvariant grace-timeout. That finding, in plain terms: the fix makes the Binance adapter tolerant of future schema versions — that's correct and vendor-aligned — but three *other* message decoders in the adapter (order-book depth, trades, candles) were written assuming the message layout never grows. If Binance someday adds a field to those messages, they could now mis-read instead of erroring. I traced the trigger: that code only runs if we subscribe to Binance *order books*, and we never do — our Binance usage is price quotes only; the only order books we consume are Polymarket's. So it's unreachable today, it came from upstream's design rather than our port, and all three reviewers agreed it doesn't block. explain the situation in plain english - why can we merge although reviewers had some findings

Sure. Here's the whole thing in plain English.

**What the reviewers found is real — but it's not about the change we're making.**

Think of the Binance adapter as having several doors. The incident happened at one door: the "load the instrument list" door, where Binance changed the message format and our code refused anything that wasn't the exact old version. These two PRs fix that door properly, and everyone — me twice, three outside reviewers — agrees the fix is correct, tested, and proven against the real captured message.

What two reviewers flagged is a *different* set of doors: three other message types (order-book depth, trade lists, candles) whose reading code was written a bit lazily — it assumes those messages will never grow a new field. If Binance someday adds a field there, that code could misread the message instead of stopping with an error. That's a genuine weakness worth fixing eventually.

**Why it doesn't block these PRs, three reasons:**

1. **We never open those doors.** Our bot only asks Binance for price quotes. The risky code runs only when you subscribe to Binance order books — and we don't, and never have. I didn't take the reviewers' word for it; I traced the code path myself to confirm what triggers it.
2. **It's not something these PRs created.** That weakness exists in the upstream NautilusTrader project's own code and predates our fix. Rejecting our PR wouldn't remove it — it would just leave us with the *incident bug* unfixed on top of it.
3. **It's about a hypothetical future event** — Binance changing those particular messages someday — not about anything happening now.

The reviewers themselves classified it exactly this way: all three said "no blocking findings," and the two who raised it labeled it "latent" and "non-blocking." In review language: a *blocker* means "this change is wrong or dangerous — don't ship." A *finding* like this one means "while reading your code, we noticed something nearby worth fixing later." The second kind gets written down and scheduled, not used to hold the fix hostage — otherwise no fix for a live outage would ever ship.

And it *is* written down: it's item one of a four-item follow-up bundle that goes into the campaign ledger the moment these merge, so it can't quietly disappear.

Meanwhile, the cost of *not* merging is concrete and current: the bot cannot trade at all until the schema fix is live. So: real findings, correctly classified, none of them about the fix itself, all of them tracked. That's why the merge is safe — and the merge queue still runs its own full test pass as the final tripwire.

Diagnosed, reproduced locally, and it's a five-minute fix for Codex. Here's the blurb to relay:

> **#1332 revision request — source-fence-static failure, root cause pinned.**
> The failing check is the runtime-literal audit inside `run_fences.py`. Two FAILs, reproduced locally at head `c9afd6a35`:
> ```
> FAIL: unclassified Bolt-v3 production literal src/bolt_v3_live_node.rs:2110
>       ("bolt-v3 live-node launch aborted: NT NodeState is Running but the trader was never started …")
> FAIL: unclassified Bolt-v3 production literal src/bolt_v3_live_node.rs:2120
>       ("bolt-v3 live-node startup shutdown grace elapsed after {trigger} …")
> ```
> The PR's two new `Display` strings for `LiveNodeTraderNotStarted` and the revised trader-not-started grace-elapsed message were never registered in `docs/bolt-v3/research/runtime-literals/bolt-v3-runtime-literal-audit.toml`. This lane first ran after un-drafting, which is why it surfaces only now.
> **Fix:** add classification entries for exactly those literals, following the existing pattern for fail-loud diagnostics (see the `startup_subscription_derivation_diagnostic_template` entries from #1316 and the launch-subprocess entries from #1310): static fail-loud operator diagnostic, reports observed runtime state, does not configure trading behavior. No code changes. Verify with `just source-fence-static` locally before pushing, and report the new head.

One process note for the record: this is the same class as the fork-compile miss — a proof lane that hadn't actually executed yet. The draft-skips-heavy-lanes default keeps creating "everything green until un-draft" surprises; worth remembering that un-drafting *is* the first full test of a PR here.

When Codex pushes, the head moves again — I'll run the supersede check (should be audit-toml-only plus nothing else) and confirm, then you approve and queue both PRs.

should we get more review or not

No — merge. Here's the honest calculus:

**What these two PRs have already survived** is the heaviest review stack this repo has ever applied: six of my review rounds across the pair (including tests I ran myself and a red proof I produced myself), three independent external models attacking the exact risk surfaces, every finding driven to fixed-or-adjudicated, and all CI green. The externals' one real discovery was a *latent, unreachable* issue — and the fact that three strong reviewers hunting adversarially came back with only that is itself the signal: the well is dry. A fourth model or a third round of mine would re-read the same diffs with diminishing odds of finding anything the first five passes missed.

**Where the remaining risk actually lives**, no amount of additional reading can reach: how Binance's real servers behave against the fixed decoder, tonight, in production. The only test for that is the boot itself — and that test is now safe by construction. Supervised, deposit-capped, $10 order cap, and after this campaign the node has three layers of "refuse to run broken instead of pretending": it won't boot mute, it won't start silently unsubscribed, and it won't idle trader-less. If anything is still wrong, the boot *tells us* instead of costing us.

**And delay has a real price:** the bot has been unable to trade since July 9, and this incident proved vendors change things on their own calendar — the longer we sit, the more likely something else drifts under us.

So: approve both with sp-reviewer, queue both. The merge queue's fresh CI is the last mechanical gate, and the supervised boot is the last real one. That boot is the review that matters now.

content.text:
All failures decoded. Three real roots — all mechanical, none touching the design — plus some infra noise and downstream cascade. And one of them is genuinely good news in disguise.

**#1331 — two fixes needed:**
1. **Missing second lockfile.** The backtesting crate is its own cargo workspace with its own `Cargo.lock`; the PR repointed that crate's dependencies to the fork but never regenerated its lockfile, so strict builds refuse (`cannot update the lock file … because --locked was passed`). My review verified the root lockfile and this crate's manifest but missed that it has a lockfile of its own — my escape, now on record.
2. **Bolt's own schema tripwire fired — exactly as designed.** A guard test pins the Binance adapter's schema version and failed with `left: 5, right: 4`. Bolt already had a tripwire for schema drift; the fork legitimately moved to 5, so the pin updates to match. That this test noticed is the system working.

**#1332 — one fix needed:**
3. **The no-trade fence caught a comment.** The live-node module has a fence forbidding any source reference to trade-triggering symbols; the PR's new *doc comments* mention `start_trader()` by name, and the scanner can't tell prose from a call. Fix: reword the comments ("before the trader is started" instead of the symbol name). The fence itself stays untouched.

The rest of the red is cascade (gate/provenance/test jobs downstream of the failed archives) and one infra flake (a setup step). Blurb for Codex:

One more real failure surfaced on #1331, and I've root-caused it while the rest of CI finishes.

**What failed:** the clippy lane's repo-governance suite, with one error: `Cargo.toml explicit test harness count must be 13, got 14`. bolt deliberately keeps a tripwire that pins how many explicit test binaries the repo declares, so adding one forces a human to acknowledge it. #1331 legitimately added a new test binary (the SBE decode test), so the pinned count must move 13 → 14 — a one-line change in `scripts/verify_ci_workflow_hygiene.py`. I swept for other copies of that pin: there are none (the self-test reads the constant from the verifier itself), and every sibling check in that suite passed, so the bump is the complete fix.

**Why we're only seeing it now:** at the previous head this same lane died in environment setup (the infra flake), so the governance check never ran — an infra-failed lane isn't a passed lane. That's also why I'm holding the Codex punch list until *every* lane settles on both PRs: I don't want a fifth surprise after the next push. The DNS warning in the same log is from an unrelated self-test fixture and is harmless.

Everything else so far is green at both new heads, including the three lanes that failed this morning (lockfile, schema pin, fence). Watcher is on; when CI settles I'll send you the complete relay blurb for Codex — likely just this one line.

content.text:
**v0.1.11 is deployed and the boot is fully healthy — the regression pair is closed against the live venue.** The bot is now live and able to trade.

What the boot proved, in order:
1. **Launch chain green** — all stages including the subprocess health probe, and the logger stayed alive for the whole runtime (the mute defect remains dead).
2. **Binance connected at 11:57:21** — "Connected to Binance Spot SBE stream pool", no version mismatch. #1331 verified against the real exchange, and spot prices are flowing into the strategy again.
3. **Trader and strategy Running at 11:57:27** — the fail-open path didn't occur, so #1332's new invariant stayed silent, which is its correct behavior on a healthy boot.
4. **Full readiness converged** — the latest evaluation shows no pricing blocks and no gate blocks, realized volatility computed. The bot will enter a position whenever its edge threshold clears, under the usual supervised caps ($10 max notional, ~$2.50 target per order, loss governor present but not enforcing).

One new finding for the books (already recorded): the strategy logs about 40,000 lines a minute, which trips journald's rate limiter — from 12:03 the system journal silently dropped most bot output while the process was perfectly healthy. I briefly chased that as a hang before finding the suppression notices. The bot's own log file and the evidence streams are the reliable channels mid-session; the journal is not. The noisy per-tick evaluation logging is worth a ledger follow-up, but it's cosmetic today.

**Current state: the box is live and trading-capable, and you're in your supervision window.** The session-two legs on the plan are: observe the first live settlement booking, then a kill/restart with an open position, then the cash reconciliation against the wallet. Tell me when you want me to check in on it, run the restart leg, or stand the service down.
